Four signoff assumptions that don’t survive the move to 3D ICsby Admin on 11-26-2026 at 10:00 am

View Profile

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: 3D IC, EDA, Siemens EDA

Key takeaways ▼

Hybrid bonding and tight die stacking break habits that served planar design well. Here is where die-by-die thinking goes wrong in parasitic extraction, and what an assembly-aware flow does instead.
Every design team carries assumptions inherited from planar design. Most of them are sound, and some are so familiar that nobody states them out loud anymore. Parasitic extraction is a good example. For decades it has been a die-level discipline: extract the die, back-annotate, close timing, check noise, sign off.
3D IC integration changes the ground rules. Products now combine logic, memory, analog and RF chiplets with silicon interposers, redistribution layers, TSVs, embedded bridges and hybrid-bonded stacks in face-to-face and face-to-back configurations. That brings shorter interconnect, higher bandwidth density and lower latency. It also quietly invalidates several assumptions that extraction methodology has long relied on. Four of them deserve a closer look.
Assumption 1: If every die is signed off, the stack is signed off
The logic is appealing: if each component is verified, the assembly should be correct by construction. But in a 3D IC, proximity itself creates new electrical behavior. In hybrid-bonded stacks, the top metal layers of adjacent dies can sit close enough that capacitive coupling across the interface affects timing and noise, as published research on face-to-face bonded 3D ICs by Peng Petranovic, Lim and colleagues has shown. TSVs couple to one another and to redistribution-layer routing. Interposer traces couple to power planes.
The electrical behavior of one die can change when another die, an interposer or a package structure is added nearby. A die signed off in isolation has been verified against an environment that will never exist in the product, and its extracted model under-represents the real loading and noise paths of the assembled system. Die-level signoff remains necessary, but it is no longer sufficient. Extraction has to become assembly-aware, capturing the electrical context that appears only once the full stack is built.
Assumption 2: Capturing system effects means extracting everything flat
Once teams accept that the assembly matters, the reflex is to flatten it and extract the whole stack as a single design. That is rarely practical. The dies may come from different process technologies, different teams and different schedules, and the combined geometry is enormous. A flat run also throws away the work already done at the die level.
The more effective approach is modular. Each die is extracted as a standalone component with its own resistive and capacitive model. A dedicated interface extraction step then computes only the capacitive coupling between conductors near the bonding interface. Finally, the standalone and interface parasitics are merged into a system-level netlist that drives static timing analysis, dynamic simulation and signal-integrity analysis. Figure 1 shows the kind of structure involved: three stacked dies with face-to-face and face-to-back bonds, BEOL routing, TSV landing pads and back-side metal.
Figure 1. Cross-section of hybrid bonding and routing across three stacked dies, including face-to-face and face-to-back interfaces, BEOL routing, TSV landing pads and back-side metal. Modular flows such as the Calibre 3D IC extraction flow extract each die separately and then target only the coupling across these interfaces. (Source: Siemens Digital Industries Software)
The interface step has one non-negotiable rule: it must not re-count what the standalone runs already captured. Tools built for this job, such as Calibre 3DStack working with Calibre xACT3D, generate interface-specific stack information, connectivity rules and annotated layout for the bonding region, and use explicit ignore mechanisms so that only the cross-die contribution is extracted. Done this way, modular extraction delivers assembly-aware results without the cost of a monolithic run.
Assumption 3: If a coupling capacitor was extracted, it is in the netlist
This is the subtlest of the four. A modular flow assumes that every conductor involved in cross-die coupling can be identified as a node in the merged netlist. For nets that reach an external port, that is true: the interface capacitor connects port to port and the merge knows exactly where it belongs.
In practice, interface conductors are often fractured – segmented by extraction, by shielding or by distributed modeling of internal connectivity. Many belong to internal nets that are never exposed at the die boundary, and some are unnamed. When the interface extractor calculates coupling to one of these conductors, the capacitor has no valid electrical node to connect to, so it is dropped. The effect is most pronounced in sparse layouts. The merged model simulates cleanly and looks complete, yet it describes only a subset of the physical coupling paths.
The remedy is to create connection points ahead of time. During standalone die extraction, the extraction tool adds ports on selected internal or unnamed nets and writes those definitions to a file that the interface preparation step can consume. Those labels are carried into the annotated layout for the stack, so when interface extraction runs, the generated ports are legal nodes and the coupling capacitors land where they belong. Figure 2 shows the situation.
Figure 2. A fractured/internal-net interface with external port-connected nets, internal nets and the resulting cross-die coupling capacitors. Without additional connection points, coupling on internal and fractured nets is lost; the Calibre 3D IC extraction flow introduces those points automatically. (Source: Siemens Digital Industries Software)
Assumption 4: One connection point per net is good enough
Even for nets that do reach an external port, a single lumped connection point can mislead. A long conductor running along the bonding interface couples to its neighbors across the whole of its length, not at one spot. Collapsing that distributed behavior into a single node may be acceptable for some digital timing checks, but it hides where the coupling actually occurs. For high-frequency links, that distinction matters.
The same port-insertion mechanism that rescues internal nets also addresses this case. Additional ports can be placed on interface nets connected to external ports, with controllable spacing between them, so the extracted model reflects spatially distributed coupling across the interface. It is a reminder that the required accuracy depends on the analysis: compact SPEF-style parasitics may serve timing closure, while signal-integrity work on high-frequency links may call for RCLK, broadband or S-parameter-oriented models.
Replacing assumptions with a method
All four assumptions held for planar designs. They break down in 3D for the same reason: much of a stacked design’s electrical behavior, including cross-die coupling, appears only after the dies are assembled.
A modular flow keeps the die-level work and adds what it misses. Each die is extracted on its own. The interface is extracted separately, without re-counting coupling that the standalone runs already captured. Generated ports give every coupling capacitor a valid place to connect, including on fractured, internal and distributed nets. The results are then merged into a system-level model for timing, noise and signal-integrity analysis. The interface parasitics in that model link component-level signoff to verification of the assembled system.
